12: The like became those muzzles filth-begrimed Of Cerberus the demon, who so thunders Over the souls that they would fain be deaf.
16: We passed across the shadows, which subdues The heavy rain-storm, and we placed our feet Upon their vanity that person seems.
20: They all were lying prone upon the earth, Excepting one, who sat upright as soon As he beheld us passing on before him.
24: “O thou that art conducted through this Hell,” He said to me, “recall me, if thou canst; Thyself wast made before I was unmade.”
28: And I to him: “The anguish which thou hast Perhaps doth draw thee out of my remembrance, So that it seems not I have ever seen thee.
33: But tell me who thou art, that in so doleful A place art put, and in such punishment, If some are greater, none is so displeasing.”
37: And he to me: “Thy city, which is full Of envy so that now the sack runs over, Held me within it in the life serene.
41: You citizens were wont to call me Ciacco; For the pernicious sin of gluttony I, as thou seest, am battered by this rain.
45: And I, sad soul, am not the only one, For all these suffer the like penalty For the like sin;” and word no more spake he.
49: I answered him: “Ciacco, thy wretchedness Weighs on me so that it to weep invites me; But tell me, if thou knowest, to what shall come
54: The citizens of the divided city; If any there be just; and the occasion Tell me why so much discord has assailed it.”
58: And he to me: “They, after long contention, Will come to bloodshed; and the rustic party Will drive the other out with much offence.
63: Then afterwards behoves it this one fall Within three suns, and rise again the other By force of him who now is on the coast.

77: Here ended he his tearful utterance; And I to him: “I wish thee still to teach me, And make a gift to me of further speech.

87: Say where they are, and cause that I may know them; For great desire constraineth me to learn If Heaven doth sweeten them, or Hell envenom.”

114: So we passed onward o’er the filthy mixture Of shadows and of rain with footsteps slow, Touching a little on the future life.

And he to me: “Return unto thy science, Which wills, that as the thing more perfect is, The more it feels of pleasure and of pain.

Albeit that this people maledict To true perfection never can attain, Hereafter more than now they look to be.”
123: Round in a circle by that road we went, Speaking much more, which I do not repeat; We came unto the point where the descent is;
127: There we found Plutus the great enemy.
130: “Pape Satan, Pape Satan, Aleppe!” Thus Plutus with his clucking voice began; And that benignant Sage, who all things knew,
132: Said, to encourage me: “Let not thy fear Harm thee; for any power that he may have Shall not prevent thy going down this crag.”
133: Then he turned round unto that bloated lip, And said: “Be silent, thou accursed wolf; Consume within thyself with thine own rage.
134: Not causeless is this journey to the abyss; Thus is it willed on high, where Michael wrought Vengeance upon the proud adultery.”
137: Even as the sails inflated by the wind Involved together fall when snaps the mast, So fell the cruel monster to the earth.
138: Thus we descended into the fourth chasm, Gaining still farther on the dolesome shore Which all the woe of the universe insacks.
139:
Justice of God, ah! who heaps up so many New toils and sufferings as I beheld? And why doth our transgression waste us so?

As doth the billow there upon Charybdis, That breaks itself on that which it encounters, So here the folk must dance their roundelay.
142: Here saw I people, more than elsewhere, many, On one side and the other, with great howls, Rolling weights forward by main force of chest.
144:
They clashed together, and then at that point Each one turned backward, rolling retrograde, Crying, “Why keepest?” and, “Why squanderest thou?”

Thus they returned along the lurid circle On either hand unto the opposite point, Shouting their shameful metre evermore.
